newsitem.title: UK: NATO applicants need support package - Denmark.
newsitem.headline: NATO applicants need support package - Denmark.

text.p: NATO should work out a major support package to help reassure those potential members who will not be among the first to be admitted to the alliance, Danish Defence Minister Hans Haekkerup said on Monday.
"It's very important that we come up with something substantial because many of those who will not be among the first new members will be very disappointed," he told reporters.

Denmark is pressing for Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania to be granted NATO membership but the three Baltic states are unlikely to be allowed in soon, in part because Moscow is fiercely opposed to the idea.
NATO defence chiefs last week said an enhanced Partnership for Peace (PFP) programme should include having officers from partner countries in NATO headquarters across Europe.
The PFP concept was agreed by NATO's 16 countries as a way of developing links with former Warsaw Pact countries such as Poland and Hungary, and with European neutrals such as Finland.

Haekerrup, who was speaking ahead of talks with British Defence Secretary Michael Portillo, said that under a new expanded PFP, potential members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation could also provide troops for peace support operations which did not involve the use of weapons.
"I think this should be offered to all partner countries who are not among the first new members, whether they seek membership or not," he said.
Russia says NATO's expansion towards its borders would threaten its security and has recently taken a more hardline approach to the affair.

Haekkerup dismissed comments by Russian Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, who said in a newspaper interview published last week that one option for responding to NATO expansion would be to point Moscow's missiles at the new eastern European members.
"This is a non-issue. Nobody in NATO would think of deploying nuclear missiles on the territory of new member states. I think it's political card-playing," he said.
"They don't want new members in NATO and by raising the question of nuclear weapons, they hope to get concessions."

Most of the former Communist PFP countries have said they want to join NATO. The decision on which countries will be invited in first -- expected to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- will be made at a NATO summit next year.
Haekkerup said Denmark wanted the summit to be specific about when the second wave of countries would be let in, but conceded he was not optimistic this would happen.
He said he thought it was unlikely that the Baltic states would be kept in permanent limbo.
"I don't think NATO will compromise on this...These countries should never be taken hostage," he said.
Earlier this month NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana tried to reassure the three Baltic states that they had not been ruled out as candidates for alliance membership.
